title: JESUS RECEIVES YOU AS YOU ARE—BUT DOES HE INTEND TO LEAVE YOU THAT WAY?
paragraphs: JESUS RECEIVES YOU AS YOU ARE—BUT DOES HE INTEND TO LEAVE YOU THAT WAY?
Grace will meet you covered in yesterday’s dirt. But if you truly encounter Jesus, grace will not make peace with the chains that are destroying you.
There is a sentence Christians love to say because it sounds like the safest place in the world:
“Come to Jesus just as you are.”
And it is gloriously true.
Come addicted.
Come ashamed.
Come angry.
Come exhausted.

Come with the marriage you helped damage, the secret you keep deleting from your phone, the bitterness nobody at church knows about, the questions you are almost afraid to ask, the habit you promised God you would quit, the memories you cannot erase, the guilt you cannot outpray, and the version of yourself you have become frighteningly good at hiding.
Come with your scandal.
Come with your failure.
Come with the evidence.
Come before you have fixed yourself.
Because if sinners had to become clean enough to approach Jesus, nobody would ever reach Him.
But there is another sentence we do not say nearly as comfortably.
Jesus receives you as you are...
but He loves you too much to leave you as He found you.
And that is where grace becomes uncomfortable.
Because some of us want a Jesus who forgives us without confronting us.
We want mercy without repentance.
A Savior without a Lord.
A cross that removes guilt but never touches our habits.
We want Jesus to rescue us from hell while leaving every throne in our hearts exactly where it was.
We want Him close enough to comfort us...
but not close enough to change us.
And maybe that is why this question matters so much:
If Jesus receives me exactly as I am, does He intend for me to remain exactly as I am?
Look carefully at the Jesus of Scripture.
He was astonishingly approachable to broken people.
Tax collectors came near Him.
Sexually disgraced people were not beyond His reach.
The morally compromised found themselves sitting at tables with Him.
People carrying histories that respectable religious society wanted nothing to do with discovered that Jesus was willing to be seen with them.
His enemies noticed it.
They were scandalized by it.
And when Jesus was criticized for eating with tax collectors and sinners, He answered with the language of a physician:
“οὐ χρείαν ἔχουσιν οἱ ἰσχύοντες ἰατροῦ, ἀλλ’ οἱ κακῶς ἔχοντες”
Ou chreian echousin hoi ischyontes iatrou, all’ hoi kakōs echontes.
“The strong do not need a physician, but those who are sick.”

Then He explains why He came: to call sinners. In a textual tradition represented by the Textus Receptus, the statement explicitly concludes with εἰς μετάνοιαν — eis metanoian — “to repentance.” Mark 2:17.
Do not miss the picture.
Jesus does not stand outside the hospital shouting at sick people for being sick.
He comes for them.
But neither does a physician walk into the room, look at the disease destroying his patient, and say, “I accept you, therefore the disease can stay.”
Acceptance of the patient is not approval of the disease.
Compassion for the wounded is not celebration of the wound.
And the grace of Jesus toward sinners is not God's permission for sin to remain their master.
That distinction may change the way you understand Christianity.
Jesus does not say, “Fix yourself, then come.”
He says, in effect, “Come.”
Then He begins doing in you what you could never accomplish without Him.
Maybe you need to hear that because you have spent years thinking you must somehow become worthy before God will want you.
You cannot scrub your history hard enough.
You cannot perform enough religious acts.
You cannot manufacture a spotless past.
You cannot undo what happened that night.
You cannot crawl backward through time and unsay those words.
You cannot unclick it.
Unbetray them.
Unwaste those years.
Uncommit that sin.
But the Gospel was never the announcement that sinners had finally discovered how to climb their way to God.
The Gospel is the announcement that God came down to rescue sinners.

Jesus Christ lived in perfect obedience, went willingly to the cross, bore sin, died, and rose again. Forgiveness is not something we purchase by becoming impressive. Salvation is God's gift received through faith, and even the good works of the Christian life are the fruit of His workmanship rather than the price paid to purchase His grace.
That is why grace can reach the person everyone else has written off.
The alcoholic.
The adulterer.
The porn addict.
The liar.
The proud churchgoer.
The angry father.
The wounded mother.
The teenager living two lives.
The preacher secretly exhausted.
The believer who fell again after promising God through tears that it would never happen again.
The person reading this who looks fine to everyone else.
Yes.
You too.
But watch what happens when grace actually takes hold of a human being.
Paul does not merely say that the forgiven person receives a cleaner record.
He writes:
Ei tis en Christō, kainē ktisis.
“If anyone is in Christ—new creation.”
Those words in 2 Corinthians 5:17 are enormous.
Καινὴ κτίσις — kainē ktisis.
New creation.
Not improved public relations.
Not religious cosmetics.
Not a Christian sticker pasted over the old identity.
New creation.
Paul continues that the old things have passed away and the new has come.
That does not mean a genuine Christian becomes instantly mature, instantly temptation-free, or incapable of stumbling.
Read the New Testament honestly and you will find believers who still needed correction, growth, discipline, endurance, confession, wisdom, and sanctification.
Christian transformation is real, but growth can be painfully uneven.
Sometimes God changes something quickly.
Sometimes He walks us through a long war.
Sometimes the chains fall dramatically.
Sometimes obedience looks like waking up tomorrow and choosing Christ again while the old temptation is still screaming your name.
The evidence of grace is not that you never struggle again.
Sometimes the struggle itself is evidence that something inside you is no longer willing to call darkness home.
Before, you could sin and settle into it.
Now something grieves.
Something fights.
Something longs for holiness.
You fall, but you cannot comfortably build a house on the ground anymore.
You begin to hate what is destroying your communion with God.
Not because you are trying to earn His love...
but because you have encountered it.
There is an enormous difference between struggling against sin and surrendering yourself to it.
There is a difference between falling in battle and signing a peace treaty with the enemy.
And somebody reading this has been confusing the two.
You failed again, so you concluded that God must be finished with you.
Listen carefully.
The answer to your failure is not hiding from Christ.
Run toward Him.
Confess.
Repent.
Get back up.
Bring the darkness into the light.
Seek wise biblical accountability where needed.
Cut off the access point you keep pretending is harmless.
Stop protecting the very thing you are asking God to deliver you from.
Grace does not tell you to hide the chains.
Grace teaches you that because Christ has come, the chains no longer have the right to name you.
This is why Romans 12:2 contains such powerful language:
“ἀλλὰ μεταμορφοῦσθε τῇ ἀνακαινώσει τοῦ νοός”
Alla metamorphousthe tē anakainōsei tou noos.
“But be transformed by the renewing of the mind.”

The word μεταμορφοῦσθε — metamorphousthe carries the idea of transformation, a change of form. Paul is not describing Christianity as merely learning how to appear more religious. The life surrendered to God is being transformed as the mind is renewed.
This is what grace does.
Grace finds Zacchaeus and generosity begins replacing greed.
Grace finds Peter after catastrophic failure and restores him.
Grace finds Saul breathing threats against Christians and turns the persecutor into a preacher of the Christ he once opposed.
The Gospel does not merely forgive people's stories.
Jesus begins rewriting them.
And now we reach the uncomfortable part.
There may be something in your life you have renamed because repentance sounded too painful.
You called bondage “just who I am.”
You called compromise “being realistic.”
You called bitterness “having boundaries.”
You called lust “normal.”
You called pride “knowing my worth.”
You called gossip “venting.”
You called greed “ambition.”
You called spiritual laziness “being busy.”
You called unforgiveness “protecting my peace.”
You called secret sin “nobody's business.”
Maybe you even called conviction “judgment” because that made it easier to silence.
But what if the ache you feel right now is not Jesus pushing you away?
What if it is the mercy of God refusing to let you become comfortable in something that is slowly destroying you?
Conviction and condemnation are not identical.
Condemnation says, “There is no hope for someone like you.”
The Gospel says, “There is hope precisely because Christ came for sinners like you.”
Conviction exposes the wound so we will stop pretending we do not need the Physician.
Jesus does not expose sin because He enjoys humiliating sinners.
He exposes darkness to bring people into light.
The cross proves both how seriously God takes sin and how profoundly God loves sinners.
At Calvary, God did not shrug at evil.
And He did not abandon humanity to it.
Christ died.
Grace was costly.
Forgiveness is free to us, but it was not cheap.
So when Jesus calls you away from sin, He is not stealing your life.
He is calling you away from what is stealing your life.
Maybe you came to Christ with pornography.
He receives the repentant sinner, but pornography does not become sacred because you became Christian.
Maybe you came with unforgiveness.
He receives you, but bitterness is not meant to become a permanent room in your heart.
Maybe you came addicted to applause, money, sexual validation, substances, control, rage, or the approval of people.
Come.
Absolutely come.
But do not confuse Christ's open arms with permission to drag your idols onto His throne.
He wants your heart.
And there is freedom in finally admitting that.
Somebody needs to stop saying, “This is just the way I am.”
Because if you belong to Christ, your past may explain some things about you...
but it no longer possesses final authority over who you are becoming.
Your trauma is real.
Your wounds matter.
Your temptations may be intense.
Your history cannot simply be pretended away.
Healing may require time, wise pastoral care, accountability, and sometimes appropriate professional help.
But none of those things change the central Christian hope:
Jesus Christ gets the final word.
Not your worst night.
Not your divorce papers.
Not the addiction.
Not the prison record.
Not the abortion.
Not the affair.
Not the abuse committed against you.
Not the abuse you regret committing.
Not the years you wasted.
Not the church people who rejected you.
Not the voice in your head telling you that you are too filthy to return.
Jesus.
The crucified and risen Christ.
He gets the final word.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to these words:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace is more powerful than denial.
Jesus can look directly at the wreckage and still say, “Follow Me.”
And following Him means movement.
You cannot follow someone while insisting that you will permanently remain exactly where you were.
Sometimes following Jesus means walking away from people who continually drag you toward destruction.
Sometimes it means confessing something you desperately want to hide.
Sometimes it means apologizing without defending yourself.
Sometimes it means deleting the number.
Closing the account.
Ending the affair.
Returning what was stolen.
Forgiving the person you wanted to hate forever.
Seeking help.
Opening the Bible when you feel spiritually numb.
Praying when heaven feels silent.
Going back to church after church hurt made you afraid to trust again.
Sometimes transformation is dramatic.
Sometimes it looks almost invisible.
One obedient decision.
Then another.
Then another.
Until one day you look behind you and realize...
Jesus has carried you farther than you thought.
You are not who you were.
Not because you became extraordinary.
Because His grace is.
That is Christianity.
Not “God accepts me, therefore nothing needs to change.”
And not “I must change enough so God will finally accept me.”
Both miss the Gospel.
The Gospel says that in Christ we are saved by grace, and the grace that saves begins producing a transformed life.
The order matters.
Grace first.
Then the life of grateful obedience flowing from grace.
We do not obey so Christ will finally love us.
We learn obedience because in Christ we have encountered a love we could never earn.
So ask yourself something uncomfortable.
Not, “Am I perfect?”
You are not.
Neither am I.
Ask this:
“Am I allowing Jesus to confront the parts of me I keep protecting from Him?”
What is the one door in your heart where you keep telling Christ, “Everywhere except here”?
What is the browser history?
The resentment?
The relationship?
The dishonesty?
The secret conversation?
The obsession?
The hidden arrogance?
The appetite?
The wound you have turned into an identity?
The compromise you keep defending because surrender would cost too much?
Maybe this article did not come across your screen merely to give you something interesting to read.
Maybe you needed the question.
Jesus receives you as you are.
But do you actually want Him to transform you?
Not polish your image.
Not improve your religious vocabulary.
Transform you.
Because there comes a moment when Christianity has to become more than content we consume.
More than verses we share.
More than worship songs playing in the background.
More than “Amen” beneath a Facebook post.
Jesus said, “Follow Me.”
And perhaps your next step begins with a painfully simple prayer:
“Jesus, I am done hiding.”
You do not have to publish the details of your private struggle. God already knows them. But sometimes three honest words are the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
Pray.
Let this become more than a comment section.
Let it become a place where wounded people discover that Christians can tell the truth about their battles while still pointing one another toward Christ.
Not because every sentence is easy to hear, but because there may be a night when temptation starts negotiating with you again and you need to remember:
Grace did not rescue you so your chains could keep you.
There may be someone quietly drowning behind a perfectly normal profile picture who will never tell you what they are fighting.
You may never know whose midnight prayer begins because you pressed “Share.”
Send this to the person who believes Christianity is only for people who already have their lives together.
Let them discover the real Gospel.
Jesus receives sinners.
Jesus forgives sinners.
Jesus restores sinners.
And Jesus transforms those who belong to Him.
It does not.
It cannot.
And not because anyone should manipulate you into giving.
Scripture explicitly guards against that. Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not be ἐξ ἀνάγκης — ex anankēs, “under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver.
Support should come from conviction, willingness, gratitude, and love.
Your support helps us keep reaching.
Keep writing.
Keep teaching.
And your sharing matters too.
Financial support is one form of partnership.
Share.
Pray.
Invite someone.
Point somebody toward Jesus.
And if you can support the work and freely choose to do so, we would be deeply grateful.
They are helping support a mission they believe in.
And everyone is invited to keep growing.
Come to Jesus.
Come now.
Not after you become respectable.
Not after you defeat every addiction.
Not after you understand the entire Bible.
Not after the shame disappears.
Not after you have repaired everything you broke.
Come with the wreckage.
Come with the confession.
Come with empty hands.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Trust Christ.
And then let the Savior who receives you begin transforming the places you thought could never change.
You may have arrived covered in scandal.
You may still carry scars.
There may still be battles tomorrow.
But scars are not the same thing as chains.
And your unfinished story is not evidence that the Author has abandoned the page.
Remember this when your past whispers your old name:
Jesus does not merely meet you in the ruins—He begins building resurrection where you thought only ruins could remain.
